We aimed to understand the awareness and attitudes of elderly Southeast Asians towards telehealth services during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic in this study.

Methods:

In this qualitative study, 78 individuals from Singapore (51.3% female, mean age 73.0 ± 7.6 years) were interviewed via telephone between 13 May 2020 and 9 June 2020 during Singapore’s first COVID-19 ‘circuit breaker’. Participants were asked to describe their understanding of telehealth, their experience of and willingness to utilise these services, and the barriers and facilitators underlying their decision. Transcripts were analysed using thematic analysis, guided by the United Theory of Acceptance Use of Technology framework.

Results:

Of the 78 participants, 24 (30.8%) were able to describe the range of telehealth services available and 15 (19.2%) had previously utilised these services. Conversely, 14 (17.9%) participants thought that telehealth comprised solely home medication delivery and 50 (51.3%) participants did not know about telehealth. Despite the advantages offered by telehealth services, participants preferred in-person consultations due to a perceived lack of human interaction and accuracy of diagnoses, poor digital literacy and a lack of access to telehealth-capable devices.

Conclusion:

Our results showed poor overall awareness of the range of telehealth services available among elderly Asian individuals, with many harbouring erroneous views regarding their use. These data suggest that public health education campaigns are needed to improve awareness of and correct negative perceptions towards telehealth services in elderly Asians.

Keywords: Attitude, awareness, COVID-19, focus groups, telehealth

INTRODUCTION

The contagiousness and virulence of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has forced several global sectors, including the healthcare, information technology and communication services sectors,[1] to radically rethink the delivery of their services.[2] This is of particular importance for health care due to the need to balance possible disease exposure risk while delivering the appropriate level of patient care. One of the most remarkable ongoing changes has been the unprecedented and accelerated expansion of telehealth.[3] Telehealth refers to the use of telecommunication technologies to connect clinicians and patients for remote delivery of health-related assessment, management and/or treatment.[4]

There is growing evidence that, compared to traditional face-to-face care, telehealth offers conveniences such as lower overall costs,[5] increased care accessibility, decreased transportation barriers,[6] and importantly, reduced spread of infectious diseases among patients and healthcare practitioners.[7] Paradoxically, and despite clear potential for benefit, the adoption of telehealth services in routine healthcare settings has been slow, often failing to keep pace with the proliferation of low-cost, widely available technologies.[8,9,10,11] The COVID-19 pandemic has, therefore, provided many healthcare systems with the necessary incentive to implement telehealth technologies on a large-scale basis.[12,13,14,15]

Achieving sustained adoption of innovative interventions in health care requires awareness, acceptance and satisfaction from the user’s perspective. Indeed, key barriers to telehealth utilisation by patients include poor digital literacy, preference for existing healthcare delivery models and concerns about privacy.[16,17,18,19] Poor digital literacy is particularly problematic in adults aged 65 years and older,[19] who form the group of people whose health has been most affected by the pandemic.[20] Indeed, previous quantitative research by our group in Singaporeans aged ≥60 years found extremely low levels (2%) of utilisation of digital medical health services (e.g. video consultations and clinical messaging applications).[21] However, an in-depth understanding of factors underpinning this low rate of utilisation is lacking, without which targeted interventions to improve utilisation rates cannot be implemented. Unfortunately, current qualitative studies have mostly been conducted in clinical samples, for example, stroke survivors,[16,17,18,19] and their results lack generalisability.

With its rapid urbanisation over the last 50 years, Singapore presents a unique opportunity to explore the level of awareness, and associated barriers and facilitators underlying the adoption of these technologies in the elderly population amidst the ready availability of telehealth equipment, infrastructure and technical expertise.[22,23] In this article, we report the results of a qualitative study that sought to understand the awareness of and attitudes towards telehealth services in a sample of multi-ethnic elderly individuals aged ≥60 years in Singapore during the COVID-19 pandemic.

METHODSStudy population

A sub-study of 668 participants from an ongoing population-based cohort of multi-ethnic older adults aged ≥ 60 years (The PopulatION HEalth ProfilE in EldeRly Singaporeans [PIONEER]) was conducted between 13 May 2022 and 9 June 2020, during which Singapore was in the midst of its first government-mandated COVID-19 ‘circuit breaker’, a period of heightened safe distancing measures adopted by the government to pre-empt escalating COVID-19 infections.[24] Individuals who had previously passed the 6-Item Cognitive Impairment Test (6-CIT)[25] to rule out severe cognitive impairment and consented to be contacted for future research at the baseline study visit were invited to participate via telephone by trained research personnel. The 6-CIT was repeated if 6 months had passed since the baseline study assessment to rule out cognitive deterioration. Chinese, Indian, Malay and Eurasian individuals who did not have hearing or speech impediments significant enough to compromise the study procedures were included.

For this qualitative study, we excluded 90 (13.5%) participants who were not able to communicate in English or Mandarin. Of the 578 eligible individuals, 113 (19.6%) declined to participate in the qualitative interviews. We then utilised an age-, gender- and ethnicity-stratified framework to purposively select 78 individuals from the remaining 465 PIONEER participants to take part in semi-structured interviews using baseline participant sociodemographic data. The study is reported according to the consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research (COREQ) guidelines.[26] As the entire study was conducted via telephone, a waiver of written informed consent was obtained from the country’s centralised ethics board, and the study protocol adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Study protocolData collection

Semi-structured interviews were conducted in the participants’ preferred language (English or Mandarin) by trained interviewers using an interview guide developed and pilot tested by the research team. The guide was designed to elicit information regarding participants’ awareness and attitudes towards telehealth (e.g. telehealth delivery models, type of telehealth services available in Singapore and experience with telehealth services). If participants had no knowledge of telehealth, a standardised explanation was provided to them with examples, after which they also answered open-ended questions on their attitudes towards telehealth, specifically whether they thought it was useful, whether they were willing to utilise telehealth in place of face-to-face consultations both during and after the end of the circuit breaker, as well as the barriers and facilitators underlying their decisions. Nondirective prompts were used to encourage more detailed information as needed. The guide was translated into Mandarin by a professional translation company and back-translated into English by trained research officers proficient in both English and Mandarin (minimum of a ‘B’ grade in both English and Mandarin as a mother tongue in the Singapore–Cambridge General Certificate of Education Ordinary Level examination) to check for accuracy. Interviews were audio recorded, with 10% of these audio recordings subjected to fidelity checks by a trained researcher (ELPX). Data collection stopped upon reaching thematic saturation, that is, no new themes emerging from the collected data.

Data analysis

Interview audio recordings were professionally transcribed verbatim and translated into English (if needed). All transcripts were checked against the original recordings for accuracy. Two coders conducted thematic analysis on participants’ responses regarding their attitudes towards telehealth services, guided by the United Theory of Acceptance Use of Technology (UTAUT) model.[27] This model is one of the most comprehensive frameworks developed to study decision-making related to technology adoption and has been utilised previously in studies on telehealth acceptance.[17,28,29] The UTAUT model assesses the strength of an individual’s intention to perform a specified behaviour and postulates that this behaviour is influenced by four main constructs/themes: Performance Expectancy (degree to which an individual believes the technology would be beneficial to his/her performance), Effort Expectancy (perceived ease of technology use), Social Influence (degree to which an individual perceives that important others [friends/family members] believe he/she should utilise the technology in question) and Facilitating Conditions (degree to which an individual believes that an organisation and/or technical infrastructure exists to support the use of the technology) [Figure 1].[27]

A representation of the United Theory of Acceptance Use of Technology model. This model aims to provide holistic insight into factors (four main domains: Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, Social Influence and Facilitating Conditions) that have an influence on the behavioural intention to use new technology.

Following Braun and Clarke’s six steps of thematic analysis,[30] the two coders first familiarised themselves with the data and then analysed them using the constant comparative method,[31] giving equal attention to each interview. Codes were developed and organised, based on conceptual similarities, into the UTAUT model themes. Codes were discussed, with any discrepancies addressed in regular meetings between the coders. If a consensus could not be reached, the first author provided adjudication, and investigator triangulation was achieved.[32]

RESULTS

Of the 78 participants selected for the interview, 40 (51.3%) were female, 36 (46.2%) were Chinese, 14 (17.9%) were Malay, 27 (34.6%) were Indian and one (1.3%) was Eurasian. The mean age (standard deviation [SD]) of the participants was 73.0 ± 7.6 years [Table 1]. A total of 69 (88.5%) participants were interviewed in English and nine (11.5%) were interviewed in Mandarin. The average length of each interview was 11.7 ± 4.8 (range 5.1–36.2) min.

Of the 78 participants, 38 (48.7%) had heard of the term ‘telehealth’; of these 38 participant, 14 (36.8%) believed that telehealth comprised solely home medication delivery services. The remaining 24 (63.2%) participants were able to describe the range of telehealth services available in Singapore, including telephone and online video consultation with healthcare practitioners for both urgent and stable chronic conditions, the ability of the practitioner to have access to the patient’s healthcare records during the teleconsultation and the ability to order and have medications delivered to their doorstep. In contrast, approximately half (n = 40, 51.3%) of the participants had not heard of telehealth before. These participants were more likely to be women and of Indian ethnicity compared to other ethnicities (P < 0.05) [Table 1].

While 15 (19.2%) participants reported having personally utilised telehealth services as part of their medical care, including stroke rehabilitation and emergency teleconsultations, the most common telehealth experience was found to be home medication delivery (13/15, 86.7%). Participants’ experience of telehealth usage was positive overall, with commendations on the proactive follow-up by participants’ consulting doctors and the personable attitudes of medication delivery personnel. However, several participants were concerned about a long waiting time for medication delivery (up to 2 weeks), especially if they were running low on their medication supply. When participants were probed further on how telehealth services could be incorporated into Singapore’s healthcare system, 38 (48.7%) participants mentioned that it would be a viable alternative to receiving medical care during periods of restricted movement (e.g. as imposed by the COVID-19 outbreak), although most of these participants (n = 21, 55.3%) expressed preference for in-person consultations once movement restrictions have eased.

Theme: Facilitating conditions

Many participants reported becoming interested in telehealth because of the COVID-19 circuit breaker restrictions. Participants with a keen interest in utilising new technology reported greater interest in adopting telehealth services to complement, or even replace, face-to-face appointments, particularly for routine review/follow-up checks or medication refills. Conversely, those who preferred to utilise telehealth services only during periods of restricted movement cited the ‘impersonal’ nature of such models as a barrier (e.g. lack of human contact).

Importantly, participants highlighted that the lack of accessibility to and high cost of devices that are capable of hosting telehealth services were major deterrents to its uptake. Other barriers to telehealth service uptake included a perceived lack of access to medical records by healthcare practitioners during teleconsultations that results in potential misdiagnoses, the higher cost of teleconsultation compared to face-to-face appointments, and fewer opportunities for exercise, as there is no need to walk/travel to the healthcare facilities when using telehealth services.

Overall, participants felt telehealth services were useful for certain populations, including the very elderly, those with mobility issues (e.g. stroke survivors) and busy working adults unable/unwilling to travel to appointments during work. Participants also opined that clinical appointments requiring minimal medical supervision, such as biochemistry (blood and urine) test review, regular reviews for stable chronic conditions (e.g. diabetes mellitus and hypertension) and medication refill, could transition entirely to the telehealth medium without any negative repercussions.

Theme: Performance expectancy

Most participants who had utilised telehealth services believed they saved time, money and resources as they did not have to travel and wait for healthcare appointments. Participants also felt that telehealth enables them to maintain independence, not rely on others for help, have greater control over their own safety (e.g., not having to travel in bad weather or when unwell), and avoid the risk of contracting healthcare-based infections. Conversely, some participants felt that the virtual medium of telehealth may potentially lead to patient–practitioner miscommunication, given the lack of nonverbal cues, such as facial expressions, which may lead to difficulties in conveying changes to treatment regimens or difficulties in describing physical signs of sickness accurately.

There was also a pervasive perception that telehealth consultations were less thorough than face-to-face consultations due to the inability to conduct a physical examination virtually. Participants were worried about the accuracy of diagnoses made based purely on verbal descriptions of symptoms and/or self-obtained clinical measures, for example, blood pressure. Moreover, they felt that doctors were more meticulous during face-to-face consultations and could respond better to new information unearthed during physical examination and questions asked by patients during the consultation.

Theme: Effort expectancy

Most participants reported that the effort needed to learn how to use telehealth-capable devices, such as those for video conferencing programmes, was a major deterrent to fully embracing telehealth services, especially in elderly participants. Similarly, several participants conveyed that their experience with telehealth services and their ability to ask for help in utilising telehealth-capable devices were key factors driving their willingness to utilise telehealth services. Participants highlighted the need to educate less digitally literate individuals in their age group on how to use these devices, via brief overviews on television programmes or in-depth face-to-face training courses on using specific telehealth devices.

Theme: Social influence

Participants unanimously acknowledged that social influence, such as newspapers and news reports, television advertisements, media publicity of telehealth service launches, online websites and Facebook posts, was seminal in their willingness to try out telehealth services. Word of mouth from friends and family members who have tried telehealth services and advice from healthcare practitioners offering these services were also cited as sources of influence in using telehealth.

Participants almost unanimously believed that awareness and knowledge of telehealth services needed to be increased in elderly individuals, particularly for those who were less digitally literate/confident to navigate cyberspace alone. Suggestions included distribution of pamphlets to each household to ensure wide coverage and unambiguous support of telehealth by healthcare practitioners. Importantly, several participants noted that their doctors expressed a preference for face-to-face appointments when they discussed the viability of utilising telehealth services with them.

DISCUSSION

In our in-depth qualitative investigation of the awareness of, and attitude towards, telehealth services among a community-based sample of elderly Southeast Asian individuals living in Singapore, nearly three-quarters of our participants had no or limited knowledge of telehealth services. While participants almost unanimously agreed that telehealth was important in allowing patients to seek medical care during strict COVID-19 movement restrictions, several major hurdles to the uptake of telehealth services were noted, including a perceived lack of human contact, reduced accuracy of diagnoses during telehealth consultations, and poor digital literacy and/or a lack of access to telehealth-capable devices due to perceived cost. Participants felt that promotion by the government and healthcare practitioners on the awareness and utilisation of telehealth services in this vulnerable population was warranted. Given the increasingly important role of telehealth services in routine medical care, these results provide a contemporary and comprehensive understanding of the reasons underpinning poor awareness and attitude towards telehealth services in elderly Southeast Asians, which will inform development and evaluation of interventions to improve uptake of telehealth services.

Over half of our participants had no awareness of what telehealth was, despite the strong digital and network infrastructure, and the availability of telehealth-capable devices in Singapore.[22,23] These results differ from the relatively high awareness rates of ~63%–78% in published data from Eastern and Central Asia,[33,34] which could be partially attributed to differences in (a) study design (qualitative study design vs. quantitative questionnaire-based surveys that did not allow for further probing)[33,34]; (b) sample population (community-based vs. clinical participants)[33]; and (c) amount of coverage given to telehealth service availability (country dependent).[34] Importantly, over half of our respondents preferred face-to-face consultations despite the presence of COVID-19 circuit breaker-related restrictions, even after telehealth services were explained to them. These findings are echoed by community and clinical quantitative studies conducted in the USA and Singapore,[21,35,36] which showed that over half of the respondents were unlikely to utilise digital health services even against the backdrop of continuing social distancing measures. To improve awareness and uptake, participants suggested advertising the availability of telehealth services on traditional news media outlets, such as newspapers and radio, and also making door-to-door visits or distribution of pamphlets to promote telehealth services, since many elderly individuals do not have a social media profile. Moreover, based on the important role of healthcare providers in increasing the awareness and uptake of telehealth services as highlighted by our participants, another strategy could involve incentivising and training healthcare providers to utilise and advertise these services as part of their care regimen. However, before adopting this strategy, it may be prudent to qualitatively evaluate healthcare providers’ acceptance and the barriers and facilitators underpinning implementation of these services into their workflow.

Many participants appreciated the time and cost savings of telehealth consultations compared to in-person consultations, a finding that was echoed by telehealth studies conducted in rural and underserved populations.[37,38] Indeed, many mentioned the importance of such services for persons with mobility issues, such as wheelchair-bound individuals and stroke survivors. Interestingly, other participants still preferred to walk to and from in-person consultations for exercise, as most residents have access to medical services within walking distance of their homes due to the relatively high density of medical practices in Singapore (20 government and over 1,700 private medical practices across a land mass of 730 m2). Some participants indicated, perhaps due to COVID-19 pandemic, that utilising telehealth services prevented them from contracting healthcare-associated infections, a common finding since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic.[39,40]

Several key barriers to telehealth uptake that were raised by the participants who were already aware of telehealth services were related to perceived communication difficulties, specifically the lack of nonverbal cues coupled with a lack of physical examination and nervousness in conveying information through a virtual medium, which has been well documented in previous telehealth and communications research.[41,42] The issue of communication is particularly egregious, with previously published studies reporting that the lack of nonverbal cues during teleconsultations has resulted in a perceived belief of a lack of attention being paid to patients’ concerns during telehealth consultations.[41] Participants’ suggestions of limiting telehealth services for appointments requiring minimal medical supervision (e.g. biochemistry test reviews) may hence be a reflection of these concerns. Until these issues are addressed, either via technological advancements and/or by targeted programmes to improve nonverbal communication, a more gradual approach to incorporating telehealth services into the existing medical system, for example, by first introducing telehealth for biochemistry test reviews, may be warranted.

Consistent with previous reports,[43,44] the high cost and limited availability of telehealth-capable devices, coupled with low digital literacy, were among the most salient barriers to telehealth utilisation raised by our participants, particularly those who were aware of these services, but did not have personal experience utilising them. This is surprising, given that almost 80% of Singaporeans aged ≥60 years own a smartphone/tablet.[45] It is possible that our respondents may not be fully aware of the capability of their smart devices; unfortunately, we did not pursue this line of questioning in our interviews. Consequently, the ability to ask for device/application help from others was a key factor driving the use of telehealth services in our respondents and, given that many elderly individuals in Singapore live either in multigenerational households or near their children, this could be leveraged upon in public outreach programmes to gain wider acceptance of telehealth among the elderly in Singapore.[46] Moreover, digital literacy programmes for the elderly, which have been documented to increase perceived digital skills and reduce anxiety,[47] were also raised as a practicable solution to improve uptake of telehealth services for this population.

The main strength of this study is its qualitative design, which allowed us to comprehensively explore the reasons underpinning participants’ responses to questions on telehealth awareness, attitudes and acceptance. Our large, purposively recruited community-based sample also enhanced the generalisability of our results to the elderly population under investigation. We also utilised the COREQ criteria to guide our study design, and data synthesis was informed by a well-accepted theoretical framework (UTAUT).

One limitation of qualitative methodology is that we were unable to identify factors associated with lack of awareness and negative attitudes towards telehealth services. Moreover, participant responses, particularly their attitudes towards telehealth services, may have been influenced by their own personal positive or negative experiences with telehealth services. In addition, the limited number of Indian, Malay and Eurasian participants and the paucity of dialect and non-English/Mandarin speakers may mean that we could have some ethnic-specific concerns. Moreover, we did not conduct qualitative interviews with healthcare providers and caregivers to garner their feedback on telehealth use in the elderly, which would have complemented our patient-centric data and informed focused strategies to improve awareness and acceptance of such services. Further, we acknowledge that this study was done relatively early in the pandemic (May 2020–June 2020), and patient perceptions on telehealth services may have changed over time, given the likely increased exposure to such services consequent to the continued social distancing measures put in place by the Singapore government. Moreover, as the population ages, there is a need to understand the awareness and associated barriers and facilitators towards uptake of telehealth services by a younger and more technology-savvy population. As such, further qualitative studies addressing these limitations may be warranted. Lastly, it may be helpful to understand the differences in attitude and awareness of those who are aware and unaware of telehealth services, an undertaking best achieved via quantitative methodology. Indeed, quantitative investigations utilising outcomes from our qualitative study to formulate categorical questions while also incorporating the appropriate statistical analyses may provide additional valuable information to complement our findings and inform future interventions to improve awareness and attitudes towards telehealth services.

In conclusion, we found a relatively low awareness of telehealth services among elderly Southeast Asian individuals. Although these individuals acknowledge the benefits of telehealth services, a reluctance to use such services over in-person consultations — due to a perceived lack of human interaction and accuracy of diagnoses, poor digital literacy and a perceived lack of access to telehealth-capable devices — was observed. As such, to maintain momentum for the adoption of telehealth services into routine medical care resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, the key issues relating to lack of awareness and negative attitudes towards these services from the perspective of the elderly need to be addressed. Healthcare provider endorsement of telehealth services via mainstream and traditional news outlets may help improve awareness, while digital literacy programmes may improve uptake and change negative perceptions towards telehealth services in our elderly Southeast Asian population.
